_meta.source: CL = Código Limpo: Habilidades Práticas do Agile Software (Robert C. Martin; Brazilian edition, Alta Books), scanned PDF of 398 pages, text by OCR
_meta.page_convention: (CL p.N) = PDF page; the printed page is not used (the offset varies across the scan)
_meta.note: rules = stated in the book with a page; not_in_book = NOT in the book (label [extrapolation]); uncovered = topics with no coverage. Prose is English; keywords keep the Portuguese search terms and add English ones.

fonte-identificacao-obra.name: Identification of the work, preface and organization of the book
fonte-identificacao-obra.summary: Cover with title, subtitle and 'Série de Robert C. Martin'; preface by James O. Coplien; introduction with the WTFs/minute figure and the division into three parts. Year, ISBN and translator do not appear in the scan.
rules: Title Código Limpo, subtitle Habilidades Práticas do Agile Software, Robert C. Martin series (CL p.1)
Preface by James O. Coplien, linking the book to TPM and the 5S (CL p.2-6)
The doors figure: the only valid measure of code quality is WTFs/minute, by Thom Holwerda (CL p.7)
Three parts: principles and practices; case studies; a chapter of heuristics and smells (CL p.8)
not_in_book: The PDF has no ISBN, edition year, cataloging data or translator's name
The WTFs/minute figure is not the author's, it is by Thom Holwerda
There is no table of contents in the scan

o-que-e-codigo-limpo.name: Definitions of clean code (Stroustrup, Booch, Thomas, Feathers, Jeffries, Cunningham)
o-que-e-codigo-limpo.summary: The author gathers definitions from six programmers: elegance and doing one thing (Stroustrup), readable prose (Booch), tests and ease of change (Thomas), care (Feathers), Beck's rules (Jeffries), code that is what you expected (Cunningham).
rules: Stroustrup: elegant and efficient, minimal dependencies, complete error handling, does one thing well (CL p.17-18)
Booch: simple and direct, reads like well-written prose (CL p.18)
Dave Thomas: another developer can read and improve it; it has tests; code without tests is not clean (CL p.19)
Feathers: looks like it was written by someone who cared (care) (CL p.19-20)
Jeffries/Beck: runs all the tests, no duplication, expresses the ideas, minimizes entities (CL p.20)
Cunningham: each routine is what you expected; the language looks made for the problem (CL p.21)
not_in_book: There is no single official definition: the book presents itself as one school of thought among others (CL p.22)
The broken windows metaphor is attributed to Dave Thomas and Andy Hunt, not to Stroustrup

custo-codigo-confuso.name: Cost of bad code and professional attitude
custo-codigo-confuso.summary: Mess drives productivity toward zero; full rewrites become years-long races; the blame lies with programmers, who must defend the code; the only way to go fast is to keep the code clean.
rules: Bad code can bring down a company (CL p.13)
Productivity drops asymptotically toward zero and adding people makes it worse (CL p.14)
The Grand Redesign can last 10 years and end in a new mess (CL p.15)
Programmers must protect the code with the same passion with which the manager protects the deadline (CL p.16)
The only way to go fast is to always keep the code clean (CL p.16)
not_in_book: The chapter does not use the expression 'technical debt' (dívida técnica)
The printed translation of LeBlanc's law is 'Nunca é tarde' (it is never too late); from context the meaning is that 'later' never comes (later equals never)

regra-do-escoteiro.name: The Boy Scout Rule
regra-do-escoteiro.summary: Leave the code cleaner than you found it; small continuous improvements prevent degradation.
rules: Code must be kept clean over time, not just written clean (CL p.24)
Leave the campground cleaner than you found it (Boy Scouts of America) (CL p.24)
The cleanup can be small: rename, split a function, remove repetition, reduce a nested if (CL p.24)
not_in_book: The rule does not tell you to rewrite whole modules; it speaks of small cleanups

somos-autores-leitura.name: We are authors: reading vs. writing
somos-autores-leitura.summary: We read far more than we write (10x1 in the text); making code easy to read makes it easy to write.
rules: A programmer is an author with readers, responsible for communication (CL p.23)
The time ratio between reading and writing is 10x1 (CL p.23)
To write quickly, make the code easy to read (CL p.23)
not_in_book: The book cites no research for the 10x1 ratio; it is based on replayed editing sessions

principios-srp-ocp-dip.name: Design principles cited (SRP, OCP, DIP) and relation to PPP
keywords: Agile Software Development Principles Patterns and Practices
principios-srp-ocp-dip.summary: The book is a prequel to PPP (2002) and cites SRP, OCP and DIP in passing, deferring the details to PPP.
rules: Sporadic references to SRP, OCP and DIP, described in detail in PPP (CL p.24)
The calculatePay switch violates SRP and OCP (CL p.47)
not_in_book: The SOLID acronym does not appear on any page
LSP and ISP are not named
The printed translation calls DIP 'Princípio da Inversão da Independência'

nomes-proposito-desinformacao.name: Intention-revealing names, without disinformation and with meaningful distinctions
nomes-proposito-desinformacao.summary: A name must say why it exists, what it does and how it is used; it must not suggest something false; different names must mean different things.
rules: If a name requires a comment, it does not reveal its purpose (CL p.27)
Do not call something List if it is not a List; avoid nearly identical names (CL p.28)
Do not use lowercase l or uppercase O as names (CL p.29)
Number series (a1, a2) and noise words (Info, Data) distinguish nothing (CL p.29-30)
not_in_book: The book does not forbid every prefix: it accepts prefixes that mark a real distinction (CL p.30)

nomes-pronunciaveis-buscaveis.name: Pronounceable and searchable names
nomes-pronunciaveis-buscaveis.summary: Names must be speakable and findable by search; the length of a name follows the size of its scope.
rules: Create pronounceable names: programming is a social activity (CL p.30)
Searchable names beat literal constants; long names beat short ones (CL p.31)
The length of a name should be proportional to the size of its scope [N5] (CL p.31)
WORK_DAYS_PER_WEEK is easier to find than the literal 5 (CL p.32)
not_in_book: It does not forbid one-letter names: it accepts them as locals in short methods (CL p.31)

codificacoes-notacao-hungara.name: Avoid encodings: Hungarian Notation, the m_ prefix, I on interfaces
codificacoes-notacao-hungara.summary: Do not encode type or scope in the name; Hungarian notation and m_ are obstacles in modern languages; prefer not to mark the interface; avoid names that require mental translation.
rules: Encoding type or scope in the name is unnecessary mental load (CL p.32)
Hungarian Notation is an obstacle today: it makes changing a name or type harder and can mislead (CL p.32)
Do not use the m_ prefix; keep classes and functions small and use an IDE that highlights members (CL p.32-33)
Do not decorate interfaces with I; if needed, encode the implementation (ShapeFactoryImp) (CL p.33)
Avoid mental mapping; i, j, k only in very small scopes (CL p.33)
not_in_book: The rule about I on interfaces is a declared personal preference ('Prefiro', I prefer), not a prohibition

nomes-classes-metodos.name: Names of classes and methods, cute names, one word per concept, puns
nomes-classes-metodos.summary: Classes are nouns and methods are verbs; use get/set/is; prefer clarity to jokes; one word per concept, but do not use the same word for different ideas.
rules: Classes use nouns; avoid Manager, Processor, Data, Info; never a verb (CL p.34)
Methods use verbs; accessors use get, set, is (JavaBean standard) (CL p.34)
With overloaded constructors, use a static factory with a descriptive name and a private constructor (CL p.34)
Do not be cute: clarity instead of fun (CL p.34)
One word per concept; do not mix fetch, retrieve and get (CL p.35)
Do not pun: an add that inserts into a collection should have another name (CL p.35)
not_in_book: It does not require English names; the translation uses translated examples (Cliente, postarPagamento)

dominio-e-contexto-nomes.name: Solution/problem domain and context in names
dominio-e-contexto-nomes.summary: Prefer technical terms known to programmers, fall back on the problem domain when there are none; give context with classes and namespaces, without excess.
rules: Use computer science terms, algorithms and pattern names (AccountVisitor, JobQueue) (CL p.35-36)
With no technical term, use the problem domain name (CL p.36)
Give context with classes, functions and namespaces; prefixes (addrState) are a last resort (CL p.36)
Variables with obscure context can become fields of a new class (Listings 2-1, 2-2) (CL p.36-38)
Do not prefix everything with the application name (GSD); short names if they are clear (CL p.38)
not_in_book: It does not say to always use business terms: the default is the solution domain, and the problem domain when there is no technical term

tamanho-de-funcoes.name: Function size, blocks and indentation
keywords: how long should a function be
tamanho-de-funcoes.summary: Functions should be small and smaller still; the translation says at most 20 lines, and the ideal shown is 2 to 4 lines; one-line blocks and indentation of at most one or two levels.
rules: First rule: functions should be small; second: smaller than that (CL p.43)
Lines of up to 150 characters; functions of at most 20 lines (CL p.43)
In Kent Beck's Sparkle program every function was 2, 3 or 4 lines, the recommended size (CL p.43)
if/else/while blocks of one line, preferably a function call (CL p.44)
Indentation level of at most one or two (CL p.44)
not_in_book: The author says he has no research to prove it: it is experience (CL p.43)
It sets no cyclomatic complexity limit

uma-coisa-nivel-abstracao.name: Do one thing, one level of abstraction and the Stepdown Rule
uma-coisa-nivel-abstracao.summary: A function does one thing if its steps are one level below its name; all statements at the same level; code read top to bottom descending one level at a time.
rules: Functions should do one thing, do it well, and do only it (CL p.44)
If you can extract another function with a name that is not a restatement of the implementation, it does more than one thing (G34) (CL p.45)
A function divided into sections does more than one thing (CL p.45)
All statements at the same level of abstraction (CL p.45)
Stepdown Rule (Regra Decrescente): read top to bottom like TO paragraphs (CL p.46)
not_in_book: The book does not use the English term 'stepdown' nor 'SLA/Single Level of Abstraction'; it calls it Regra Decrescente

switch-polimorfismo.name: Switch statements and polymorphism
switch-polimorfismo.summary: A switch always does N things; hide it in an abstract factory that creates polymorphic objects and use it only once.
rules: A switch by nature does N things (CL p.46)
The calculatePay switch grows, does more than one thing, violates SRP and OCP and is repeated in other functions (CL p.47)
Hide the switch in an ABSTRACT FACTORY and dispatch by polymorphism (CL p.47)
Acceptable if it appears once, to create polymorphic objects, hidden behind inheritance [G23] (CL p.47)
not_in_book: It does not forbid switch in an absolute way; the author admits breaking the rule sometimes (CL p.47)

nomes-descritivos-funcoes.name: Descriptive function names
nomes-descritivos-funcoes.summary: Long, descriptive names beat short enigmatic ones and comments; try several; keep phrasing consistent in the module.
rules: A long descriptive name is better than a short enigmatic name and than a long comment (CL p.48)
Try several names; the search for names leads to restructuring the code (CL p.48)
Use the same phrases, nouns and verbs in the function names of the module (CL p.48)
not_in_book: It sets no maximum length for names

parametros-de-funcoes.name: Arguments: count, monads, dyads, triads, flags, objects and lists
parametros-de-funcoes.summary: Ideal is zero, then one and two; avoid three; more than three only for a very special reason. Boolean flags indicate the function does two things. Group arguments into objects.
rules: Zero is ideal; then monad, then dyad; avoid triad; polyad requires very special justification (CL p.48)
Monads: a question about the argument, a transformation with a return, or an event (CL p.49)
A boolean argument (flag) is ugly: split into two functions, e.g. renderForSuite/renderForSingleTest (CL p.49-50)
Dyads cost more; convert to a monad when possible; Point(0,0) is natural (CL p.50)
Think hard before creating a triad (CL p.50)
More than two or three arguments: group them in a class (makeCircle(Point, radius)) (CL p.398)
Varargs treated equally count as one list argument; String.format is a dyad (CL p.398)
Monad as verb/noun pair; the keyword form puts the argument names in the function name (CL p.398, p.51)
not_in_book: The book does not forbid dyads: it says you will certainly have to use them (CL p.50)
Printed page 42 is at PDF p.398, out of order

efeitos-colaterais-saida-cqs.name: Side effects, output arguments and command-query separation
efeitos-colaterais-saida-cqs.summary: Side effects are lies and create temporal coupling; avoid output arguments; a function does something or answers something, not both.
rules: Side effects are lies; a checkPassword that initializes the session creates temporal coupling (CL p.51)
If the coupling is necessary, the name must say so (CL p.51-52)
Avoid output arguments; in OO change the state of the object itself (report.appendFooter()) (CL p.52)
A function should do something or answer something, but not both (CL p.52)
Split a set that returns a boolean into attributeExists and setAttribute (CL p.53)
not_in_book: The book does not use 'Command Query Separation' nor 'CQS'; it uses 'Separação comando-consulta'

excecoes-try-catch.name: Exceptions instead of error codes; extract try/catch
excecoes-try-catch.summary: Prefer exceptions to error codes; extract try/catch into their own functions; error handling is one thing; error enums become dependency magnets.
rules: Returning an error code slightly violates command-query separation and causes nesting (CL p.53)
Extract the try/catch bodies into functions of their own (CL p.54)
Error handling is one thing: try is the first statement and nothing comes after catch/finally (CL p.54)
The Error enum is a dependency magnet; new exceptions derive without recompiling everything (CL p.54-55)
not_in_book: The chapter does not address checked vs. unchecked exceptions; that is left to the error handling chapter (another group)

duplicacao-evite-repeticao.name: Avoid repetition (duplication)
duplicacao-evite-repeticao.summary: Duplication may be the root of all evil in software; the algorithm repeated four times in Listing 3-1 was unified in the include method.
rules: Duplication bloats the code and requires several changes when the algorithm changes (CL p.55)
Duplication may be the root of all evil in software (CL p.55)
Normalization, OO, structured programming, AOP and components fight duplication (CL p.55)
not_in_book: Ch. 3 does not use the DRY acronym; it appears in other chapters (CL p.178, p.284, p.324)

programacao-estruturada-return.name: Structured programming (Dijkstra) and multiple returns
programacao-estruturada-return.summary: The one-entry, one-exit rule helps little in small functions; occasional return, break and continue are acceptable; avoid goto.
rules: Dijkstra: one entry and one exit; one return, no break/continue, never goto (CL p.55)
In small functions, occasional return/break/continue cause no problem (CL p.55-56)
goto only makes sense in large functions, so avoid it (CL p.56)
not_in_book: The book does not require a single return

como-escrever-funcoes.name: How to write functions like this (process)
como-escrever-funcoes.summary: The author first writes long, ugly functions, with tests covering everything, and then refines them; he does not apply the rules from the start. Functions are the verbs of the domain language.
rules: Writing code is like writing prose: first a draft, then refinement (CL p.56)
Refine with unit tests passing: split, rename, remove duplication (CL p.56)
The rules are not applied from the start; the author thinks that is impossible (CL p.56)
Functions are the verbs and classes the nouns of the system's language (CL p.56)
not_in_book: The book does not require writing the clean function in the very first version

comentarios-filosofia.name: Comments: the central thesis (comment as failure)
comentarios-filosofia.summary: Comments are at most a necessary evil: they make up for a failure to express ourselves in code, they age and they lie. Prefer cleaning up and naming well.
rules: A comment makes up for the failure to express ourselves in code; before commenting, try to express it in code (CL p.60)
Inaccurate comments are worse than none; the truth is in the code (CL p.60)
Do not comment bad code: clean it (CL p.60-61)
Replace the comment with a function whose name says the same (e.g. isEligibleForFullBenefits) (CL p.61)
not_in_book: The book does not forbid all comments: it lists 8 kinds of good comments (CL p.61-65)
It does not use the term 'self-documenting code' (código autodocumentado)

comentarios-bons.name: Good Comments (8 kinds)
comentarios-bons.summary: The book accepts eight kinds: Legal, Informative, Explanation of Intent, Clarification, Warning of Consequences, TODO, Amplification and Javadocs in Public APIs.
rules: Legal Comments (Comentários Legais): copyright/authorship at the top; reference a standard license instead of transcribing the terms (CL p.61)
Informative Comments (Informativos): useful, but prefer a function name that carries the information (CL p.62)
Explanation of Intent (Explicação da intenção): record the why of a decision (CL p.62-63)
Clarification (Esclarecimento): only for code you cannot change; check the accuracy (CL p.63)
Warning of Consequences (Alerta Sobre Consequências): e.g. slow test, SimpleDateFormat not thread-safe (CL p.64)
TODO comment: does not justify bad code; review and eliminate regularly (CL p.64-65)
Amplification (Destaque): highlights something important that seems irrelevant (CL p.65)
Javadocs in Public APIs (Javadocs em APIs Públicas): write them well; they can be as misleading as other comments (CL p.65)
not_in_book: It does not mention FIXME, only TODO
It defines no TODO format beyond // TODO

comentarios-ruins.name: Bad Comments (18 kinds)
comentarios-ruins.summary: List of 18 headings: Mumbling, Redundant, Misleading, Mandated, Journal, Noise, Scary noise, Don't use a comment when you can use a function or variable, Position markers, Closing brace comments, Attributions and bylines, Commented-out code, HTML, Nonlocal information, Too much information, Inobvious connection, Function headers, Javadocs in nonpublic code (printed in Portuguese: Murmúrio, Redundantes, Enganadores, Imperativos, Longos, Ruidosos, Ruídos assustadores, ..., Créditos e autoria, Explicação do código em comentários, ...).
rules: Mumbling (Murmúrio): if you comment, do it well; a comment that forces you to read another module has failed (CL p.65-66)
Redundant Comments (Redundantes): do not repeat the code (Listings 4-1, 4-2) (CL p.66-68)
Misleading Comments (Enganadores): inaccuracy about behavior induces error (CL p.69)
Mandated Comments (Imperativos): requiring a Javadoc on every function or a comment on every variable is silly (CL p.69)
Journal Comments (Longos): a changelog/diary at the top of the module should be removed; version control keeps that (CL p.69-70)
Noise Comments and Scary Noise (Ruidosos e Ruídos assustadores): obvious or copied with errors; refactor instead of venting (CL p.70-72)
Do not use a comment if you can use a function or a variable (CL p.72-73)
Position Markers (Marcadores de Posição): rarely and sparingly (CL p.73)
Closing brace comments: shorten the functions (CL p.73)
Attributions and bylines (Créditos e autoria): leave it to version control (CL p.74)
HTML Comments, Nonlocal Information, Too Much Information, Inobvious Connection, Function Headers, Javadocs in Nonpublic Code (CL p.75-77)
not_in_book: The names 'atribuições' or 'informação demais' are not the Brazilian edition's headings: they are 'Créditos e autoria' (p.74) and 'Informações excessivas' (p.76)

codigo-comentado.name: Commented-out code
codigo-comentado.summary: Lines of code disabled in a comment pile up like dirt because nobody dares delete them; delete them, version control remembers.
rules: Delete commented-out code; source control keeps it (CL p.74-75)
In Ch. 17 the equivalent heuristic is C5: Código como comentário (commented-out code) (CL p.282)
not_in_book: The heading 'Explicação do código em comentários' (p.74) is the translation of 'Commented-Out Code'; it is not about explaining code in prose

javadoc.name: Javadoc: when yes and when no
javadoc.summary: Good in public APIs; bad when imposed by rule on every function and in non-public code.
rules: Write good javadocs for public APIs (CL p.65)
A mandatory-Javadoc-on-every-function rule produces abominations (Listing 4-3) (CL p.69)
Javadocs in non-public code are clutter and distraction (CL p.77)
HTML in comments is the tool's job, not the programmer's (CL p.75)
not_in_book: It does not address JSDoc, docstrings or XML doc; only Javadoc

exemplo-gerador-primos.name: Final example: GeneratePrimes / PrimeGenerator
exemplo-gerador-primos.summary: Listing 4-7 shows a 'well documented' module full of bad comments; Listing 4-8 is the refactored version with only two justifiable comments.
rules: GeneratePrimes was created for the first XP Immersion as an example of bad programming and comments (CL p.77)
In the refactored version two comments remain: the algorithm header and the justification of the square root (CL p.78-80)

formatacao-objetivo-e-equipe.name: Purpose of formatting and team rules
formatacao-objetivo-e-equipe.summary: Formatting is communication, the first rule of the professional. In a team a single agreed style applies, enforced by a tool.
rules: Formatting is communication and matters more than 'making it work' (CL p.82)
Choose simple rules, apply them consistently; in a team, a single set; ideally automated (CL p.82)
Team rules: the rules belong to the team; in FitNesse they were defined in 10 minutes and configured in the IDE formatter (CL p.95)
Uncle Bob's formatting rules: illustrated in Listing 5-6 (CodeAnalyzer) (CL p.95-97)
not_in_book: It does not cite linters or formatters by name
It does not prescribe tabs vs. spaces or indentation size

formatacao-vertical.name: Vertical formatting (file size, newspaper, distance, ordering)
formatacao-vertical.summary: Small files (~200 lines, up to 500), read like a newspaper; blank lines separate concepts; what is related stays close; caller above callee.
rules: Seven projects analyzed; FitNesse: average ~65 lines, maximum ~400; systems with files of ~200 lines and a limit of 500 (not a fixed rule) (CL p.82)
Newspaper metaphor: high level at the top, details descending (CL p.83)
Vertical openness between concepts: blank lines between thoughts (CL p.83-84)
Vertical density: related lines together, with no useless comments in between (CL p.84-85)
Vertical distance: related concepts close; local variables near use, loop variables inside the loop (CL p.85-86)
Instance variables in a well-known place, in Java at the top of the class (CL p.86)
Dependent functions: caller above callee (CL p.87)
Conceptual affinity: more affinity, less distance (CL p.89)
Vertical ordering: dependencies point downward (CL p.89-90)
not_in_book: 200/500 lines is not a mandatory limit
The name 'Regra Decrescente' (Stepdown Rule) is from Ch. 3 (CL p.46)

formatacao-horizontal.name: Horizontal formatting (line width, spacing, alignment, indentation)
formatacao-horizontal.summary: Short lines (average ~45 characters; the author uses 120 as the limit); spaces show relationship and precedence; do not align in columns; always indent, even small scopes.
rules: Lines are about 45 characters; widths from 20 to 60 add up to 40%; ~30% are under 10 (CL p.90)
Hollerith's 80 limit is arbitrary; 100 or 120 acceptable; the author uses 120; do not shrink the font to fit 200 (CL p.90)
Space around assignment; no space between function name and '('; space after commas (CL p.91)
Spaces indicate precedence: factors together, terms separated (CL p.91)
Horizontal alignment does not help; long lists indicate a class to split (CL p.92-93)
Indent every scope; do not collapse short if/while/functions into one line (CL p.93-94)
Tiny scopes: the semicolon of an empty while on its own line and indented (CL p.95)
not_in_book: It does not fix 80 columns
It defines neither tabs nor 2/4 spaces

abstracao-de-dados.name: Data abstraction (getters/setters)
abstracao-de-dados.summary: Hiding the implementation is not putting getters/setters over variables; it is exposing abstract interfaces that manipulate the essence of the data.
rules: Private variables exist so nobody depends on them; automatic getters/setters expose them (CL p.98)
An abstract interface (Point) hides whether the representation is rectangular or polar and enforces atomic writes (CL p.99)
Prefer getPercentFuelRemaining() to gallon getters: express the data abstractly (CL p.99-100)
The worst option is to add getters/setters carelessly (CL p.100)
not_in_book: It does not forbid getters/setters; it criticizes adding them without thinking (CL p.100)

antissimetria-dados-objetos.name: Data/object anti-symmetry (procedural vs. OO)
antissimetria-dados-objetos.summary: Objects hide data and expose behavior; data structures expose data and have no behavior. Procedural makes new functions easy; OO makes new types easy.
rules: Objects hide data behind abstractions and expose functions; data structures expose data and have no meaningful functions (CL p.100)
Procedural: adding a function is easy (shapes do not change); adding a structure requires changing all the functions (CL p.101-102)
OO: adding a class is easy; adding a function requires changing all the classes (CL p.101-102)
Want new types: objects/OO; want new functions: data structures and procedures (CL p.102)
Everything being an object is a myth (CL p.102)
Choose without prejudice the approach that best fits (CL p.106)
not_in_book: It does not say OO is always superior (CL p.102)
It does not use the term 'expression problem'

lei-de-demeter.name: The Law of Demeter
lei-de-demeter.summary: A method f of class C should only call methods of C, of objects created by f, of f's parameters and of objects in C's instance variables; not of objects returned by those calls.
rules: A module should not see the insides of the objects it manipulates (CL p.102)
f of C only calls methods of: C; an object created by f; an object passed as a parameter to f; an object in an instance variable of C (CL p.102)
Do not call methods of objects returned by the permitted calls: talk to friends, not to strangers (CL p.103)
Only applies to objects; data structures naturally expose their structure (CL p.103)
not_in_book: It does not cite the origin/authors of the law; it only points to Wikipedia (CL p.102)
It does not forbid all dot chaining (CL p.103)
It does not use 'Princípio do Menor Conhecimento' (Principle of Least Knowledge)

carrinhos-de-trem.name: Train wrecks
carrinhos-de-trem.summary: Chains such as ctxt.getOptions().getScratchDir().getAbsolutePath() are sloppy; breaking them into variables helps, but whether it is a violation depends on them being objects or data structures.
rules: Call chains (train wrecks) are sloppy and should be avoided [G36] (CL p.103)
In general, split the chain into intermediate variables (CL p.103)
If they are objects, knowing the internals violates Demeter; if they are data structures, it does not (CL p.103)
Accessors confuse the matter; public fields in data structures would clarify it (CL p.103)
G36 'Evite a navegação transitiva' (avoid transitive navigation) revisits the topic (CL p.301)
not_in_book: It does not say that fluent APIs/builders violate Demeter (topic not addressed)

hibridos-e-estruturas-ocultas.name: Hybrids and hidden structures (tell, don't ask)
hibridos-e-estruturas-ocultas.summary: Hybrids (behavior + exposed data) are the worst of both worlds. If it is an object, tell it to do something instead of navigating its structure.
rules: Hybrids make it hard to add functions and structures; avoid creating them (CL p.104)
